name: LibSourcey (icey) HTTP server
baseline: Go net/http (go1.25.0) and Node.js http (v20.19.5); raw libuv+llhttp C server as the ceiling
workload: Single-threaded HTTP/1.1 server returning an empty 200 OK, driven by wrk -t4 -c100 -d10s on one vCPU, in two modes: Connection: close and keep-alive.
claimed_speedup: Keep-alive: icey 72,209 req/s (1.43 ms avg latency) vs Go 1.25 net/http 53,878 req/s (2.31 ms) and Node.js v20 45,514 req/s (3.56 ms); the README says it outperforms Go by 34% and Node.js by 59% and reaches 75% of raw libuv+llhttp (96,088 req/s, 1.04 ms). Connection: close: icey 14,330 req/s (8.19 ms) vs Go 14,723 req/s (6.28 ms) vs Node.js 9,309 req/s (10.71 ms), i.e. icey roughly ties Go (slightly behind) and beats Node.js by about 1.5x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DBUILD_PERF=ON -DENABLE_LOGGING=OFF; compiler name and version not stated (project requires GCC 12+ or Clang 15+). Go built with go build, Node run as is.
hardware: 11th Gen Intel Core i7-11800H @ 2.30GHz, 1 vCPU, Linux 6.8.0-106-generic x86_64; wrk 4.1.0 on the same machine
tradeoffs: Large multi-module media stack (libuv, FFmpeg, OpenSSL, llhttp, libdatachannel); LGPL licence; the HTTP server is one module of the toolkit. Keep-alive wins come from a lean single-threaded libuv event loop with no GC or goroutine scheduler.
caveats: First-party, one machine, compiler and version not stated, so this falls one detail short of tier A. The repo moved from sourcey/libsourcey to nilstate/icey and the project was renamed icey. The server and load generator share a single vCPU, which favours the lightest runtime and may disadvantage Go's goroutine scheduler and Node. Workload is an empty 200 response with Content-Length: 0, not a realistic handler. With Connection: close icey is slightly slower than Go (14,330 vs 14,723 req/s), and raw libuv+llhttp is 33% faster than icey on keep-alive (96,088 vs 72,209). The Go and Node servers are the minimal stdlib examples checked in at src/http/perf/go-server.go and node-server.js. README headline table reports keep-alive only; the Connection: close table is in src/http/perf/README.md.

name: libsrt (srt_vector sort)
baseline: std::sort (GNU/Clang std::vector sort) and C qsort()
workload: Sorting srt_vector contents: 8-bit elements by counting sort, 16/32/64-bit elements by in-place MSD binary radix sort; compared with qsort() and sorting a C++ std::vector.
claimed_speedup: README: 8-bit elements O(n) counting sort, 'much faster than GNU/Clang qsort() (C), and up to 5x faster than GNU/Clang std::vector sort (C++)'; 16/32/64-bit elements '2x-3x faster than GNU/Clang qsort() (C), performing similar to GNU/Clang std::vector sort (C++)'. doc/benchmarks.md also says srt_hmap hash maps are on average 2x-5x faster than libsrt's own tree srt_map (internal comparison, not against the STL).
tradeoffs: C library with its own string, vector, bitset, set, map and hash map types; vector sort is only specialised for 8, 16, 32 and 64-bit element types, generic elements fall back to qsort(); concurrent read/write needs user locking; maps keep nodes in one linear block with index links; deletion is slower than insertion.
caveats: First-party README sentence with no table, no input sizes, no compiler, flags or CPU stated; the 'GNU/Clang' wording does not say which C++ standard library (libstdc++ or libc++) was used, so baseline_stdlib is left empty. The 5x is an 'up to' figure and applies only to 8-bit elements, where a counting sort is O(n) against a comparison sort, an easy win; for 16/32/64-bit elements the README says libsrt only performs similar to std::vector sort (beats qsort() by 2x-3x). doc/benchmarks.md carries complexity notes only, no timings, and says some functions (e.g. vector) are not yet optimised. The repo has a bench executable (make -f Makefile.posix bench, CPP11=1 for the STL hash map comparison) but no published results. Lead URL faragon.github.io/libsrt.html was not opened (*.github.io is blocked in this environment); the repo README on github.com was used instead. Listed under the allocators-gcs guess, but the project is a data-structure and string library, so it is filed under sorting.
